cards.title: Introduction to REST APIs
cards.content:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It relies on a stateless, client-server, cacheable communications protocol — and essentially all of HTTP is used.

In Flask, we can build RESTful APIs easily by returning JSON responses.

options.text: GET is used to create new resources.
POST is typically used to create new resources.
PUT is used exclusively for deleting resources.
DELETE cannot be used in a Flask application.

cards.title: Returning JSON in Flask
cards.content:
To send JSON data back to the client in Flask, we use the jsonify function.

from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/api/hello', methods=['GET'])
def hello():
    return jsonify(message="Hello, World!")

content.instructions: Order the steps of a typical Flask REST API request lifecycle from start to finish.

items.text: Client sends an HTTP request to a specific route URL.
Flask router matches the URL pattern to a view function.
The view function processes the request and interacts with data.
Flask returns a serialized JSON response back to the client.

cards.title: Handling Incoming JSON Data
cards.content:
When clients send data to a POST or PUT endpoint, it usually arrives as JSON. We use request.get_json() to access this data in Flask.

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/api/items', methods=['POST'])
def create_item():
    data = request.get_json()
    item_name = data.get('name')
    return jsonify({"created": item_name}), 201

cards.title: REST API Best Practices
cards.content:
Key takeaways for building REST APIs in Flask:

  • Use plural nouns for resource endpoints (e.g., /api/users instead of /api/getUser).
  • Leverage appropriate HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
  • Always return correct HTTP status codes alongside your JSON payloads.
